powder.mainRisk: defamation - name living people only with charges, filings or rulings

in: big-tech scandals with a money mechanism
corporate lawsuits and regulator cases (series: The Trial)
non-violent heists and money mysteries (series: Where Did the Money Go)
China-US corporate fights (chip bans hitting a company)
out: personal finance advice or stock tips
allegation-only stories without filings or charges

backlog.name: Enron
backlog.angle: Off-books partnerships hid debt until the share price fell from about $90 to pennies in 2001; the auditor went down with it.

backlog.name: Wirecard
backlog.angle: Auditors could not find EUR 1.9bn of cash in 2020; the German payments star was insolvent within days.

backlog.name: FTX
backlog.angle: Customer deposits went to a sister trading firm; the exchange was bankrupt in about nine days in November 2022.

backlog.name: Theranos
backlog.angle: A blood-test startup valued at $9bn whose machines did not work; the founder was convicted of defrauding investors.

backlog.name: Lehman Brothers
backlog.angle: The accounting trick called Repo 105 and the largest bankruptcy in US history, September 2008.

backlog.name: WorldCom
backlog.angle: Ordinary running costs booked as investments; internal auditors found about $11bn of fake profit in 2002.

backlog.name: Luckin Coffee
backlog.angle: Fabricated sales of about RMB 2.2bn, exposed by an anonymous research report in 2020.

backlog.name: Nikola
backlog.angle: An electric-truck maker whose famous 'driving' video was a truck rolling downhill; the founder was convicted of fraud.

backlog.name: Evergrande
backlog.angle: China's biggest property developer defaulted in 2021 with more than $300bn of liabilities.

backlog.name: Satyam
backlog.angle: In 2009 the chairman admitted the books showed about $1bn of cash that did not exist; often called India's Enron.

backlog.name: Bernie Madoff
backlog.angle: A Ponzi scheme with about $65bn of paper balances that ran for decades until the 2008 crash made clients want their money.

backlog.name: Adelphia
backlog.angle: A cable company whose founding family borrowed billions through hidden loans; bankrupt in 2002.

backlog.name: Tyco
backlog.angle: Top executives took unapproved bonuses and company-paid luxuries worth about $150m; the CEO was convicted in 2005.

backlog.name: Greensill Capital
backlog.angle: A supply-chain finance lender that collapsed in 2021 and pulled a steel group down with it.

backlog.name: Archegos
backlog.angle: A family office used hidden leveraged swaps; its 2021 margin calls cost the banks more than $10bn.

backlog.name: Silicon Valley Bank
backlog.angle: A bank run that took about two days in March 2023 after bond losses and a tech-only customer base.

backlog.name: Carillion
backlog.angle: The UK government contractor that collapsed in 2018 with a pension hole and optimistic accounting.

backlog.name: Toshiba accounting scandal
backlog.angle: Profits overstated by about $1.2bn over years because bosses set targets nobody could refuse.

backlog.name: Olympus
backlog.angle: Decades of hidden investment losses; the CEO who asked questions was fired in 2011.

backlog.name: Parmalat
backlog.angle: An Italian dairy giant claimed a EUR 4bn bank account that was forged, 2003.

backlog.name: Valeant
backlog.angle: Huge drug-price increases and a secret pharmacy network; the share price lost about 90% in 2015-16.

backlog.name: Steinhoff
backlog.angle: A South African retail empire whose accounting irregularities in 2017 wiped out most of its value.

backlog.name: 1MDB
backlog.angle: A Malaysian state fund where billions were diverted and the bank that sold its bonds was fined.

backlog.name: Barings Bank
backlog.angle: One trader hid losses in an error account and a 233-year-old bank was sold for GBP 1 in 1995.

backlog.name: Long-Term Capital Management
backlog.angle: A star hedge fund with huge leverage needed a Wall Street rescue in 1998.

backlog.name: Bre-X
backlog.angle: A gold 'discovery' in Indonesia built on salted samples; the stock collapsed in 1997.

backlog.name: WeWork
backlog.angle: From a $47bn valuation to a pulled IPO in 2019 and bankruptcy in 2023.

monitor: S&P Global Market Intelligence monthly US bankruptcy report

powder.audience: 25-54, ~75% male, US/UK/CA/AU/IN; business students, investors, tech workers, 'how did nobody notice' viewers; watches MagnatesMedia, Coffeezilla, ColdFusion, How Money Works
titlePatterns: The [Object] That Sank a $[N] Billion Company
thumbnailPatterns: white miniature boardroom/office, one red mannequin (decision-maker) or one red document
optional small credited photo-pin of the real executive in a corner
company logo as a small label tag
monochrome world + one red subject, readable at TV and phone size

shorts.rules: own written hook line per Short via script-writer, end card to full film, never a raw slice; Shorts are discovery only

partition.niche: Geo-economics of borders, chokepoints and trade routes
partition.tagline: The lines on the map that move money
partition.mainRisk: war-adjacent topics can get limited ads - non-graphic imagery, neutral titles, no war words in thumbnails

in: straits, canals and chokepoints (Hormuz, Suez, Panama, Malacca, Bab-el-Mandeb, Bosphorus)
rare earths, chips and critical minerals
partitions and splits of countries/regions and their cost
trade-related espionage and smuggling (series: The Smugglers)
out: religion or ethnicity conflicts as the main topic
anything that needs real combat footage
Ukraine content that could read as exploiting, dismissing or condoning the war

backlog.name: Strait of Hormuz
backlog.angle: A 21-mile-wide strait through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil passes.

backlog.name: Strait of Malacca
backlog.angle: The narrow lane between Malaysia and Indonesia that carries most of China's oil imports.

backlog.name: Suez Canal and the Ever Given
backlog.angle: One stuck ship in 2021 blocked a route used by roughly an eighth of world trade.

backlog.name: Panama Canal
backlog.angle: A freshwater-lake canal whose drought limits in 2023 forced ships to queue or sail around.

backlog.name: Bab-el-Mandeb
backlog.angle: The gate to the Red Sea; when ships avoid it they sail around Africa and freight rates move.

backlog.name: The Bosphorus
backlog.angle: A strait through a city of 15 million that a 1936 treaty keeps open to merchant ships.

backlog.name: Danish straits
backlog.angle: The exit from the Baltic that carries Russian oil exports past Denmark.

backlog.name: Strait of Gibraltar
backlog.angle: A 9-mile gap between two continents and one of the busiest shipping lanes.

backlog.name: Taiwan Strait
backlog.angle: The shipping lane that a large share of the world's container ships and chip supply depend on.

backlog.name: Torkham and the Durand Line
backlog.angle: A colonial-era border that splits Pashtun trade and now decides when trucks cross between Pakistan and Afghanistan.

backlog.name: India-Bangladesh enclaves
backlog.angle: About 160 tiny pieces of land inside the other country, swapped in 2015 after decades of border trouble.

backlog.name: Kaliningrad
backlog.angle: A Russian exclave inside the EU whose rail transit needs permission from Lithuania.

backlog.name: Northern Sea Route
backlog.angle: The Arctic shortcut between Asia and Europe that melting ice is slowly opening.

backlog.name: Darien Gap
backlog.angle: The 100 km of jungle where the Pan-American road simply stops, and why it was never built.

backlog.name: Rhine low water
backlog.angle: Germany's main cargo river, where low water at Kaub in dry summers cuts barge loads and lifts prices.

backlog.name: Kiel Canal
backlog.angle: The busiest artificial waterway in the world, built so ships can skip the Danish straits.

backlog.name: Lombok Strait
backlog.angle: The deep-water back door that big ships use when Malacca is too shallow or too crowded.

backlog.name: Mississippi River barges
backlog.angle: The corridor that moves most US grain exports, and what low water does to farm prices.

backlog.name: Nord Stream
backlog.angle: Pipelines that bound Germany's energy supply to Russia and ended in a 2022 blast.

backlog.name: Druzhba pipeline
backlog.angle: A Soviet-era oil pipeline that still passes through Ukraine to Hungary and Slovakia.

backlog.name: Power of Siberia
backlog.angle: The pipeline that points Russian gas at China instead of Europe, and the price dispute behind it.

backlog.name: Gwadar Port
backlog.angle: A Chinese-built port in Pakistan meant to shorten China's route to the Gulf.

backlog.name: Port of Piraeus
backlog.angle: How a Greek port became a Chinese-owned gateway to Europe.

backlog.name: Hambantota Port
backlog.angle: A Sri Lankan port leased to China for 99 years after the loans could not be repaid.

backlog.name: Kra Canal
backlog.angle: The canal Thailand has debated for centuries to bypass Malacca.

backlog.name: Channel Tunnel
backlog.angle: The fixed link where border checks and a few strikes can stop UK-EU freight.

backlog.name: Trans-Siberian Railway
backlog.angle: The rail route that carries China-Europe freight overland when the sea is blocked.

partition.audience: 22-55, mostly male, US/UK/IN/CA/AU/DE; geography and world-affairs fans, logistics/energy professionals, students; watches Johnny Harris, RealLifeLore, Wendover, CaspianReport, Peter Zeihan, WGOWS
titlePatterns: The [N]-Mile Line That Controls [Share] of the World's [Thing]
Why [Place] Suddenly Matters to [Everyone / Your Wallet]
What Happens to a [Ship/Price/Factory] When [Line Closes]
thumbnailPatterns: white paper map or tilt-shift miniature port/strait from above
one red ship, red pipeline or red border line
bold map number (21 MILES, 20% OF OIL)
no explosions, burning flags or soldiers

beats: this one line on the map... (single map move)
what one ship crossing costs (number reveal)
shorts.rules: own written hook line per Short via script-writer, end card to full film, never a raw slice; same-day topical Shorts allowed when built from existing sets with a new script line
